summary:
1. WHAT DID WE BUILD?
TerraTrace turns NASA satellite data into something anyone can use.
One global map. 145,596 power facilities. 226 countries and territories.
Pick a facility. See its surroundings. Explore rainfall, soil moisture, land surface temperature and vegetation, all in one place.
No file formats. No data wrangling. 
2. HOW DOES IT ANSWER NASA'S CHALLENGE?
NASA asked us to be Earth system trend detectives. So we built five steps:
Discover. Observe. Compare. Quantify. Understand.
Find the place. Read the satellite record. Compare periods. Measure the change. See it clearly, with sources, units and observation periods.
Our prototype delivers this.         
3. WHY DOES IT MATTER?
Environmental change doesn't announce itself.
A region gets hotter. Vegetation fades. Rainfall shifts. You can't see it in a single photo. You need time.
NASA gave us the data. We made it usable, for researchers, planners, students and decision-makers.
Environmental evidence. Easier to find. Easier to understand. Easier to act on.
details:
Terra Trace: Satellite Evidence, Real Accountability

What does the project actually do?

1. Maps global energy infrastructure

Visualizes 145,596 power-facility records across eight categories, with search, filters, markers, clustering and facility details.

2. Connects facilities to historical and real time data

Uses NASA IMERG rainfall estimates, NASA GPM, MODIS, SMAP, POWER and Landsat associated with the geographical grid cells containing facilities.

3. Displays available soil-moisture information

Integrates NASA SMAP-derived surface, root-zone and profile soil-moisture , rainfall, soil moisture, temperature and vegetation information, linked to each facility. The existing global facility snapshot is not a continuous historical record.

4. Processes environmental trends

Backend modules normalize satellite observations, generate monthly time series, estimate linear slopes and compare historical periods for a selected region.

5. Presents information through one interface

Combines the React/Leaflet frontend with FastAPI services so geographical and environmental information can be accessed without manually processing satellite files.

How does it work?

-> NASA Earth Observation Data

GPM · SMAP · MODIS · Landsat · NASA POWER

-> Data Acquisition & Processing

Satellite readings, quality filtering, geographical association

Scientific Analysis & FastAPI

Time series, historical comparisons, environmental endpoints

->TerraTrace Web Application

Search · Select · Inspect · Understand

->The satellite-processing backend also uses Sentinel observations from European Copernicus missions.

What benefits does TerraTrace offer?

Intended impact

TerraTrace aims to support more informed environmental monitoring, research, public understanding and preliminary infrastructure screening. It is not a substitute for environmental impact assessments, local measurements or legal approvals.

What technologies did we use?

What makes TerraTrace creative?

Its creative contribution is the combination of three things that are often separate: where infrastructure exists, what Earth's observations tell us, and how people can explore that information.

It transforms a scientific workflow into a geographical discovery experience. Facility-based navigation provides an intuitive starting point, while the backend's modular design makes the system extensible to additional environmental variables and scientific tests.

What factors did we consider?

The team considered scientific validity, satellite quality flags, differences in spatial and temporal resolution, geographical accuracy, missing measurements, data-source credibility, scalability and ease of use.

An especially important distinction is between observed change and proven causation. TerraTrace can show that an environmental indicator changed, but that alone does not prove a nearby industry caused the change.

The same principle applies to statistical significance. Your current backend calculates descriptive trends and comparisons; it does not yet justify claiming that every detected change is statistically significant.
